paras: The attempted lynching of Juan Morales took place on August 14, 1881, when a group of would-be lynchers pursued Morales, accused of a fatal shooting at Tempe, Arizona Territory, as a constable rode with him to the jail at Phoenix. The constable lodged Morales in jail a few minutes before the pursuers arrived, and Morales was later bound over to the grand jury. A Phoenix telegram carried the story to Pacific Coast dailies as a 'Narrow Escape from Lynching'; the local press reported the man killed and the accused both as Mexicans.

According to an account the Phoenix Gazette obtained from Constable Manuel Gallardo, the dead man, whom it called Juan Nagrels, had come to Tempe about six weeks earlier and was said to have been a lieutenant of the Marquez bandits. The Gazette said his attentions to the wife of Santos Morales had roused her husband's jealousy, and that Morales forbade him the house and complained to the constable. No action could be taken, the paper explained, because Tempe had no justice of the peace at the time.

In the Gazette's telling, Morales returned home on Sunday morning to find his wife talking with Nagrels, told him he would take the law into his own hands, then drank 'forty-rod whisky' and armed himself with a six-shooter. At about four o'clock he met Nagrels in Gallardo's saloon in the upper town of Tempe, announced that he would kill him, and shot him as he ran; the second ball struck above the shoulder blade, and Nagrels died within two minutes. The Phoenix dispatch told the shooting more briefly, saying Morales killed Joaquin Negreles 'while drunk' or 'in a drunken row.'

The same dispatch reported that 'a gang of lynchers was immediately organized' and pursued the prisoner, who was in Constable Gallardo's charge and 'riding for his life.' Gallardo lodged Morales in the jail at Phoenix a few minutes before the pursuers came up, and the Sacramento copy closed with the line 'The prisoner is safe.' None of the reports names the pursuers, gives their number, or says what they did after reaching Phoenix.

Two weeks later the Arizona Weekly Citizen noted that 'Morales, the Tempe murderer,' had been bound over without bail to await the action of the grand jury. No report of an indictment or trial, or of any action against the pursuers, appears in the coverage.

The Phoenix telegram of August 15 ran the next day in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union under 'Homicide—Narrow Escape from Lynching,' in the Daily Los Angeles Herald among other Arizona dispatches, and in the Eureka Daily Sentinel under 'The Killing of Joaquin Negreles.' The Record-Union's front news summary reduced the story to a killing 'in a drunken row' and left out the lynchers. Arizona weeklies picked up the dispatch later, the Arizona Sentinel on August 20 and the Arizona Weekly Citizen on August 21.

The local Gazette account, reprinted by the Weekly Arizona Miner on August 19, was the fullest and drew on the arresting officer, but it said nothing about a pursuit. It framed the killing as a domestic drama, calling Nagrels 'the destroyer of his domestic peace and happiness' and his death 'another victim to jealousy and strong drink.' None of the papers commented on the lynchers or treated the pursuit as a matter of race.

The dispatch named the men Juan Morales and Joaquin Negreles, while the Gazette called them Santos Morales and Juan Nagrels. The dispatch attributed the shooting to drunkenness, whereas the constable's account described a planned act of jealousy, and only the dispatch reported a pursuit by lynchers.

bases: The Phoenix dispatch reports that 'a gang of lynchers' pursued an accused killer in a constable's charge, who reached the Phoenix jail first (A2, A4, A6); no one was harmed.

Morales was lodged in the Phoenix jail before the pursuing 'gang of lynchers' arrived, and no one was killed (A2, A4); this was at most an attempted lynching, and the accused and the dead man are both described as Mexicans (A5).

The homicide is reported both by the Phoenix wire and by the Gazette's independent interview with the arresting constable (A2, A5), but the pursuit by lynchers appears only in the one Phoenix dispatch and its copies (A2, A4, A6, A7); the Gazette account does not mention it (A5).
